svg.title: AAA for network devices: the flow, TACACS+ against RADIUS, and the three anti-patterns that undo both
svg.desc: Top left: the AAA flow. An engineer on a bastion host authenticates to the device, which forwards to the TACACS+ server, which consults the directory group and returns a per-command authorization decision; accounting records every command to a collector that the device cannot edit. Top right: the comparison. TACACS+ uses TCP 49, encrypts the whole payload, and supports per-command authorization - correct for device administration. RADIUS uses UDP, encrypts only the password, and authorizes at session level - correct for network access, wrong for CLI administration. Both can coexist: TACACS+ for devices, RADIUS for 802.1X. Bottom: three anti-patterns. A shared local administrator account used by the whole team, which makes accounting worthless and turns every departure into a password rotation for the estate. No accounting at all, so the only record of a change is the change ticket, which is written by the person who made the change. A fallback that authenticates locally with the same username and a weaker password, which means the attacker only needs to make the AAA server unreachable - and a flood is enough to do that. A footer states that authorization without accounting is a lock with no log, and that the fallback design is the part most often decided by accident.
svg.text: AAA on network devices: the flow is simple, the failure modes are cultural
Three letters, one requirement: every change is attributable to a person who is still employed here.
authentication: who are you - from the directory, never a local database
authorization: which commands - evaluated per command, not per session
accounting: what was done - shipped off the device, tamper-evident
the device keeps a local fallback only for the break-glass account, in a sealed envelope
use both, for their own jobs - not one for everything
one account, whole team, password in
at the default, no collector attached
the only record of a change is the ticket,
written by the person who made it
local user with the same name and a
the attacker only has to make the AAA
server unreachable - a flood will do it
Authorization without accounting is a lock with no log: it stops the wrong command and cannot tell you it happened. Both, or neither is worth the effort.
Fallback design, spelled out: break-glass credential in a sealed envelope, use triggers an alarm to the security team, and the credential is rotated the same day it is used.
Review question: name the last change made to the core and who made it. If that takes longer than a minute, accounting is decorative.
